paths.title: Web Platform & Browser Fundamentals
paths.description: Understand navigation, parsing, rendering, origins, storage, browser lifecycle, developer tools, and progressive enhancement.
topics: Client-side trust boundary
Frontend code executes in a user-controlled browser and cannot safely hold authoritative secrets or permission decisions.
Keep secrets and authorization on trusted servers while using the browser for presentation, local interaction, and non-authoritative validation.
URL anatomy
A URL combines scheme, authority, path, query, and fragment components with distinct routing and security semantics.
Use URL and URLSearchParams instead of manual concatenation when reading or constructing application URLs.
Navigation request cycle
Browser navigation coordinates name resolution, connections, HTTP requests, redirects, response handling, and document creation.
Inspect the Network panel when navigation fails so transport, cache, redirect, and response errors are separated from rendering defects.
HTML parsing and resource discovery
HTML is parsed incrementally while linked styles, scripts, fonts, images, and modules can affect when content becomes usable.
Put critical structure early and avoid parser-blocking resources unless strict execution order genuinely requires them.
DOM, CSSOM, layout and paint
Browsers derive visual output through DOM/CSSOM processing, style calculation, layout, paint, and compositing.
Measure rendering costs before optimizing and avoid unnecessary synchronous layout reads followed by writes.
Main-thread responsiveness
Long synchronous JavaScript can delay input, rendering, and other browser work even when network loading is fast.
Split expensive work, defer noncritical tasks, and move suitable CPU-heavy operations to workers.
Origin and same-origin policy
Scheme, host, and port define an origin, and browsers restrict many cross-origin reads to isolate sites.
Configure intentional cross-origin access on the server and never treat CORS as authentication or authorization.
Browser storage choices
Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, and Cache Storage differ in lifetime, capacity, synchronization, and security.
Choose storage according to sensitivity, size, offline needs, and server synchronization rather than convenience.
Feature detection and progressive enhancement
Browser capabilities vary, and resilient experiences preserve a usable baseline when an optional feature is unavailable.
Detect required APIs or CSS features and provide fallbacks instead of relying on user-agent strings.
Developer-tools evidence
Elements, Console, Network, Sources, Performance, Application, and Accessibility panels expose different layers of browser behavior.
Use the panel that matches the suspected subsystem and preserve concrete evidence such as request details, computed styles, or traces.
codeExamples:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1">
  <script type="module" src="./app.js"></script>
</head>
<body><main id="app"></main></body>
</html>

paths.title: Semantic HTML & Document Structure
paths.description: Build meaningful documents with headings, landmarks, links, media, tables, metadata, disclosures, dialogs, and native semantics.
topics: Heading hierarchy
Headings communicate nested content structure independently of visual styling.
Choose heading levels from document relationships and style them with CSS rather than skipping levels for appearance.
Landmark regions
header, nav, main, aside, and footer identify major page regions for navigation and comprehension.
Use landmarks for genuinely distinct regions and keep one clear main content area per document.
Links versus buttons
Anchors navigate to resources while buttons execute commands in the current interface.
Use an anchor with href for navigation and a button for actions so native keyboard and accessibility behavior is preserved.
Lists and grouped content
Ordered, unordered, and description lists encode relationships among repeated or paired items.
Use list markup when items form a true list instead of recreating bullets or numbering with arbitrary containers.
Image alternatives
Alternative text communicates the purpose of informative images when visual content cannot be perceived.
Write concise purpose-equivalent alt text, use empty alt for decoration, and avoid duplicating nearby captions.
Data tables
Tables represent two-dimensional relationships and need headers that identify rows or columns.
Use caption, th, scope, and simple structures so relationships remain understandable without visual position alone.
Document language and metadata
Language, title, viewport, canonical hints, and related metadata influence pronunciation, indexing, presentation, and navigation.
Set an accurate lang and meaningful route-specific title, and keep metadata synchronized with actual content.
Native disclosure and dialog
details/summary and dialog provide built-in semantics that are difficult to reproduce correctly from generic div elements.
Prefer native disclosure patterns and manage dialog focus, close behavior, and return focus explicitly.
Embedded content
Iframes create nested browsing contexts with accessibility, performance, privacy, and capability concerns.
Give frames useful titles, restrict capabilities with sandbox when possible, and avoid loading unnecessary third-party embeds.
ARIA restraint
ARIA supplements semantics when native HTML cannot express a needed role, state, or relationship, but it does not add missing behavior automatically.
Prefer native elements first and use ARIA only with the keyboard, focus, and state-management behavior the pattern requires.

paths.title: Forms & Native Controls
paths.description: Design accessible forms around labels, input semantics, validation, autofill, submission, files, and failure handling.
topics: Form task boundaries
A form should represent one coherent user task with a clear submission outcome.
Keep related controls together and separate unrelated actions so validation and status messages remain understandable.
Accessible labels
Every form control needs an accessible name, normally through a label associated with its id.
Use label for/id or an implicit label wrapper and never rely on placeholder text as the only label.
Input types and keyboards
Specialized input types communicate expected data and can improve mobile keyboards and built-in validation.
Choose email, url, tel, number, date, search, and other types only when their semantics match the field.
Names and submitted values
Successful controls with name attributes contribute values to native form submission.
Align stable name attributes with the server contract and do not assume an element id is automatically submitted.
Autocomplete semantics
Standard autocomplete tokens help browsers and password managers fill identity, address, and credential fields accurately.
Use recognized tokens and avoid disabling autofill globally, especially for usernames and passwords.
Constraint validation
required, minlength, maxlength, pattern, min, max, and input types provide useful client-side constraints.
Use native constraints for immediate feedback while keeping authoritative business validation on the server.
Actionable validation errors
Users need to know which field failed, why it failed, and how to correct it without losing entered data.
Associate messages with controls, preserve values, focus or summarize errors appropriately, and avoid color-only indicators.
Grouped choices
fieldset and legend communicate a shared question for radios or related checkboxes.
Use radio buttons for one-of-many choices and checkboxes for independent or multi-select choices.
Submission state and duplication
Slow requests can produce repeated activation, stale buttons, and duplicate operations.
Expose a pending state, prevent accidental repeated activation, and make server-side mutation handling idempotent where duplication matters.
File inputs and sensitive data
Browser file controls expose user-selected files, while credentials and personal data require careful transport and retention.
Validate file content and size on the server, use HTTPS, and keep sensitive values out of URLs, analytics, and client logs.
codeExamples:
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

paths.title: CSS Foundations, Cascade & Architecture
paths.description: Master the cascade, specificity, inheritance, box sizing, custom properties, layers, logical properties, units, overflow, and scoping.
topics: Cascade resolution
The cascade evaluates origin, importance, layers, specificity, scope, and source order to choose winning declarations.
Use computed-style tooling to identify the actual winner instead of escalating specificity blindly.
Specificity discipline
Specificity is only one cascade dimension and high selector weight makes future overrides harder.
Prefer low-specificity class or attribute selectors and avoid routine ID selectors or deeply nested chains.
Inheritance
Some properties such as color and font commonly inherit while layout properties usually do not.
Use inheritance intentionally for shared presentation and explicitly define component-specific layout constraints.
Box sizing
content-box excludes padding and border from declared dimensions, while border-box includes them.
Adopt border-box where predictable component sizing is desired and verify third-party widgets before applying global rules.
Custom properties
CSS variables participate in the cascade and can represent design tokens or contextual component inputs.
Name semantic tokens such as --surface and --space-md and override them at meaningful scope boundaries.
Cascade layers
@layer lets teams order resets, base styles, components, utilities, and third-party CSS without specificity wars.
Define layer order once and place imported or utility styles in the intended layer.
Logical properties
Logical dimensions and spacing adapt to writing direction and writing mode rather than assuming left and right.
Prefer inline/block logical properties where layouts should support localization or vertical writing modes.
Fluid constraints
min(), max(), clamp(), min-width, and max-width express ranges without a breakpoint for every size.
Use fluid constraints for typography and layout while keeping readable minimum and maximum values.
Overflow and stacking
Overflow, containing blocks, and stacking contexts explain many clipping and z-index defects.
Diagnose the responsible scroll container or stacking context instead of hiding overflow or using extreme z-index values.
CSS scoping and maintenance
Naming conventions, CSS Modules, scoped styles, and @scope constrain where rules apply.
Choose one clear scoping strategy, keep globals intentionally small, and delete obsolete overrides rather than accumulating exceptions.
codeExamples:
.title { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 3rem); margin-block: 0 1rem; }
.panel { inline-size: min(100%, 70rem); margin-inline: auto; }

paths.title: Layout: Flexbox, Grid & Positioning
paths.description: Use normal flow, Flexbox, Grid, intrinsic sizing, alignment, positioning, container queries, and stress testing for robust layouts.
topics: Normal flow
Block and inline formatting provide a resilient default layout before specialized layout modes are introduced.
Keep primary content in normal flow when possible and opt into positioning only for relationships normal flow cannot express.
Flexbox axes
Flexbox distributes items along a main axis and aligns them across a cross axis.
Use Flexbox for one-dimensional rows or columns and identify the active axis before changing alignment properties.
Flex sizing
flex-basis establishes starting size before grow and shrink distribute available space.
Set basis and min-size intentionally, especially when long content must be allowed to shrink without overflow.
CSS Grid tracks
Grid defines explicit or implicit rows and columns using fixed, flexible, and intrinsic track sizing.
Use Grid for two-dimensional alignment instead of simulating columns through nested margins or fixed widths.
Responsive repeat tracks
repeat(auto-fit, minmax()) can create fluid collections without hard-coded column counts.
Choose a meaningful minimum item size and let the grid add or remove tracks as the container changes.
Intrinsic sizing
min-content, max-content, fit-content, and intrinsic contributions allow content to influence layout.
Use intrinsic sizing when text or media should participate in geometry instead of guessing pixel dimensions.
Positioning models
relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning use different containing blocks and flow behavior.
Reserve absolute or fixed positioning for overlays and anchored UI, and diagnose ancestor overflow when sticky positioning fails.
Container queries
Container queries let reusable components respond to the size or style of their containing context.
Use container queries for cards and panels that appear in multiple layout regions rather than tying all adaptation to viewport breakpoints.
Subgrid and alignment
Subgrid lets nested content participate in parent track alignment, while gap provides relationship-owned spacing.
Use subgrid for repeated internals that must align across siblings and gap instead of special first/last margin rules.
Layout stress testing
Real layouts must survive long text, translations, zoom, large fonts, narrow screens, and missing media.
Test extreme content and at least 200% zoom before treating a responsive layout as complete.
codeExamples:
.toolbar { display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:.75rem; align-items:center; }
.toolbar__search { flex:1 1 16rem; min-inline-size:0; }
